old: Physicians speak of medicine (bheṣaja) as having four limbs and sixteen parts; what was called "sixteen-qualitied" in the previous chapter, that medicine, applied with rational planning (yukti), is capable of health: so said the venerable Punarvasu Ātreya.
new: Physicians speak of medicine (bheṣaja) as having four limbs and sixteen parts; what was called "sixteen-qualitied" in the previous chapter, that medicine, applied with rational planning (yukti), is sufficient for health: so said the venerable Punarvasu Ātreya.
why: reviewer (minor): "alam ārogyāya" is "sufficient / able (to bring) health"; "capable of health" is unidiomatic and slightly off.

old: "Maitreya, it is wrongly thought," said Ātreya. "What is the reason? What was said, that patients die though provided with this medicine endowed with sixteen qualities, is untenable; for in diseases curable by medicine, medicine is not a non-cause. And as for patients who recover without complete medicine, it is not that for them there is no special recovery for the provision of complete medicine; for just as a man raising a fallen man who is capable of rising might lend him his strength, and he would rise more quickly and without strain, so are patients through obtaining complete medicine. And as for patients who die even with complete medicine, not all of them, provided with medicine, would recover; for not all diseases are curable by means, nor is there success without the means for diseases curable by means, nor is this collection of medicine for incurable diseases; for a knowledgeable physician is not able to raise a patient who is about to die. For those who act after examination are the skilled; just as an archer who knows the technique (yoga) and is constant in practice, taking up the bow and shooting an arrow at a large target not too distant, does not miss, and accomplishes the desired task, so the physician endowed with his own qualities and equipped, having examined and beginning the action, without fault, surely endows the patient with a curable disease with health. Therefore medicine is not indistinguishable from non-medicine."
new: "Maitreya, it is wrongly thought," said Ātreya. "What is the reason? And as for patients who recover without complete medicine, it is not that for them there would be no special (better) recovery from the provision of complete medicine; for just as a man raising a fallen man who is capable of rising might lend him his strength, and he would rise more quickly and without strain, so are patients through obtaining complete medicine. And as for patients who die even with complete medicine, not all of them, provided with medicine, would recover; for not all diseases are curable by means, nor is there success without the means for diseases curable by means, nor is this collection of medicine for incurable diseases; for a knowledgeable physician is not able to raise a patient who is about to die. For those who act after examination are the skilled; just as an archer who knows the technique (yoga) and is constant in practice, taking up the bow and shooting an arrow at a large target not too distant, does not miss, and accomplishes the desired task, so the physician endowed with his own qualities and equipped, having examined and beginning the action, without fault, surely endows the patient with a curable disease with health. Therefore medicine is not indistinguishable from non-medicine."
why: reviewer (minor): Literal "for the provision of" makes the double negative nearly unreadable; the sense (stated in the draft's own note) is a better recovery resulting from complete medicine.

old: The four kinds are those of units 9 to 10 (easily curable, curable with difficulty, palliable, to be rejected).
